deckTitle: Edexcel B A-Level Economics Theme 1 Flashcards

topics.title: Role of Banks in the Economy

cards.front: Define scarcity, the economic problem.
cards.back:
Scarcity — the situation where people's wants are unlimited but the resources available to satisfy them are finite.

Scarcity is not the same as poverty. Because resources cannot stretch to meet every want, someone has to decide how they are used.

cards.front: Define a trade-off.
cards.back:
Trade-off — giving up some of one thing in order to have more of another.

Scarcity means every use of a resource rules out another use of it, so every choice involves a trade-off. A car maker with one factory can build more electric models only by building fewer petrol ones.

cards.front: Define opportunity cost.
cards.back:
Opportunity cost — the benefit given up from the next best alternative when a choice is made.

The price tells you what you pay; the opportunity cost tells you what you go without. In an answer, name the one alternative that would otherwise have been chosen, not a list.

cards.front: Define a production possibility frontier (PPF).
cards.back: Production possibility frontier (PPF) — a curve showing the largest combinations of two goods an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed.

cards.front: Sketch a PPF for capital goods and consumer goods. What does a point on the curve, a point inside it and a point outside it each show?
cards.back:
On the curve (A, C, D, B): all the economy's resources are used, so making more of one good means making less of the other. Moving from C to D gains consumer goods at the opportunity cost of the capital goods given up.

Inside (E): some resources are unemployed, so output of both goods could rise with no opportunity cost.

Outside (F): out of reach with today's resources and technology.
cards.svgAlt: Bowed-out production possibility frontier for capital goods and consumer goods, with points on the curve at A (0 consumer goods, 100 capital goods), C (100, 95), D (190, 50) and B (200, 0), point E inside it and point F outside it

cards.front: Along a PPF, moving from A to C gains 100 consumer goods for 5 capital goods, C to D gains 90 for 45, and D to B gains 10 for 50. Calculate the opportunity cost of one extra consumer good for each move. What does the pattern show?
cards.back:
A to C: 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05 capital goods per consumer good.

C to D: 45 ÷ 90 = 0.5 capital goods.

D to B: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 capital goods.

The opportunity cost of each extra consumer good rises as the economy moves down the curve. Resources are not equally good at everything, so the last ones switched across are the least suited to making consumer goods. That is why a PPF bows outwards.

cards.front: Apply opportunity cost to a consumer, a producer and the government, with one example of each.
cards.back:
• Consumer — spending £40 of wages on a gig ticket costs the trainers you were saving towards. Income and time are limited.
  • Producer — a bakery that fills its ovens with sourdough loaves gives up the croissants those ovens could have baked. Premises, staff and finance all have other uses.
  • Government — building a new hospital costs the next best project, such as new schools. Public services may be free to use, but they are not free to provide.

cards.front: Define profit maximisation.
cards.back:
Profit maximisation — producing the output and charging the price that make the gap between total revenue and total costs as large as possible.

Profit is the reward to the owners. In a company it pays shareholders their dividends and pushes up the share price.

cards.front: Define sales maximisation.
cards.back:
Sales maximisation — selling as many units as possible without making a loss, so the business at least breaks even.

To sell more, a firm usually has to charge less, so it gives up some profit per unit.

cards.front: Define satisficing.
cards.back:
Satisficing — aiming for a satisfactory level of profit that keeps the owners happy, instead of the most profit possible.

Small businesses satisfice too: an owner may be happy with a comfortable income and decide an extra few thousand pounds of profit is not worth working every weekend.

cards.front: Besides profit maximisation, sales maximisation and satisficing, the spec lists seven other business objectives. Name each and say what it means.
cards.back:
• Survival — staying in business: covering costs and having the cash to pay bills when they fall due.
  • Market share — increasing the firm's sales as a percentage of the total sales in its market.
  • Cost efficiency — producing the same output with fewer resources, so the cost of each unit falls.
  • Return on investment — the profit an investment earns as a percentage of what it cost.
  • Employee welfare — looking after staff through fair pay, training, safe conditions and job security.
  • Customer satisfaction — meeting or beating what customers expect on quality, service and value.
  • Social objectives — aims that benefit society or the environment.

cards.front: State the formula for return on investment.
cards.back:
Return on investment is the profit an investment earns as a percentage of what it cost. £1,500 profit from £10,000 invested is a 15% return.

Owners and lenders compare returns when deciding where to put their money. A project earning less than a savings account is hard to justify.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: why might a large company satisfice instead of maximising profit?
cards.back:
Shareholders own a large company, but salaried managers run it: the divorce of ownership and control. As long as profit keeps shareholders happy, managers can chase their own goals, such as a higher salary. So the business aims for a satisfactory profit, not the most profit possible.

This is the principal-agent problem, with the owners as principals and the managers as their agents.

cards.front: Evaluate sales maximisation as an objective. Why might a business give up profit per unit to sell more, and what does it cost?
cards.back:
Reasons to accept the trade-off

  • A bigger share of the market makes the firm harder to ignore, for customers and for suppliers.
  • Higher output can bring economies of scale, lowering the cost of each unit over time.
  • Low prices can put off new firms thinking about entering the market.
  • Managers' pay and status often rise with the size of the business they run, not with its profit.

The cost

  • To sell more, a firm usually has to charge less, so profit per unit falls: market share and profit can clash.

cards.front: Which objective is each business most likely to put first: a start-up, an established firm and a mature firm? What can change it?
cards.back:
• Start-up — survival, since start-ups often fail in their first few years.
  • Established firm — may chase market share.
  • Mature firm — more likely to target profit.

A recession or a new competitor can push even a large firm back to survival. In the exam, use the firm's age, size, ownership and market from the extract to explain why one objective fits it better than another.

cards.front: Define a stakeholder.
cards.back:
Stakeholder — any person or group with an interest in a business, because its decisions affect them or their decisions affect it.

Shareholders are only one kind of stakeholder, so keep the two words apart in answers. The spec also calls stakeholders economic agents.

cards.front: Distinguish internal from external stakeholders, with examples of each.
cards.back:
Internal stakeholders are inside the business: owners, managers and employees.

External stakeholders are outside it but still affected: customers, suppliers, lenders, the local community and the government.

cards.front: What does each internal stakeholder want from a business?
cards.back:
• Owners and shareholders — profit, dividends and a rising share price. Sole traders also want a decent income and some independence.
  • Managers — higher salaries and bonuses, promotion, status and job security, often linked to how big the business grows.
  • Employees — good pay, safe working conditions, training, and confidence that their job will still be there next year.

cards.front: What does each external stakeholder want from a business?
cards.back:
• Customers — low prices, good quality, reliable service and a choice of products.
  • Suppliers — regular orders, fair prices and being paid on time.
  • Lenders — interest paid and loans repaid in full, so they want the business to stay solvent.
  • Local community — local jobs and spending, with as little noise, traffic and pollution as possible.
  • Government — tax revenue, employment and growth, and firms that obey the law on wages, safety, competition and the environment.

cards.front: Define corporate social responsibility (CSR).
cards.back:
Corporate social responsibility (CSR) — a business taking account of the effects of its decisions on society and the environment, and not just on its owners, beyond what the law requires.

Examples include paying suppliers in developing countries a fair price, cutting packaging and carbon emissions, and funding local projects.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: why can a pay rise put shareholders and employees in conflict?
cards.back:
Pay rise → higher wage costs → lower profit → smaller dividends for shareholders.

Automated checkouts run the chain the other way: a lower wage bill and higher profit for shareholders, but fewer jobs for staff.

The root cause is scarcity: a business cannot give every group everything it wants, so more for one stakeholder often means less for another.

cards.front: A business plans a new distribution warehouse next to a village. Why might the local community both gain and object?
cards.back:
The local community wants local jobs and spending, with as little noise, traffic and pollution as possible. The warehouse delivers the first but threatens the second.

New warehouse → local jobs, but also lorries on village roads and lost green space → residents oppose the planning application. The firm and the community clash over expansion.

cards.front: Define an entrepreneur.
cards.back:
Entrepreneur — a person who spots a business opportunity, brings together the resources needed to exploit it and accepts the risk that it might fail.

Organising land, labour and capital and taking the risk is enterprise, the fourth factor of production. If the business works, the entrepreneur's reward is profit. If it doesn't, they can lose what they put in.

cards.front: Define creative destruction.
cards.back:
Creative destruction — the process by which new products, methods and firms replace older ones, as resources move away from businesses that have fallen behind and into new ones.

The idea comes from Joseph Schumpeter, who argued that this constant churn is how capitalist economies grow. The entrepreneur drives it.

cards.front: Define added value.
cards.back:
Added value — the selling price of a product minus the cost of its inputs.

Added value is not profit: it still has to pay for costs such as the owner's time, advertising and delivery. Profit is whatever is left after those too.

cards.front: A café owner makes three decisions: changing tomorrow's menu prices, opening a second café in the next town, and launching a lunch delivery service for local offices. Which is operating, which expanding and which developing the business?
cards.back:
Operating: changing tomorrow's prices, a day-to-day decision.

Expanding: the second café, producing more of what already works. It usually needs finance, which adds debt or brings in new owners.

Developing: the delivery service, which changes what the business does. This is where innovation happens, and where the risk of getting it wrong is highest.

cards.front: Define a social enterprise.
cards.back:
Social enterprise — a business that trades to tackle a social or environmental problem and reinvests most of its profit in that aim.

A social entrepreneur still needs revenue above costs, but the surplus pays for the mission. The Big Issue, founded in 1991, is a UK example.

cards.front: Name the four non-financial motives for starting a business that the spec lists.
cards.back:
• Ethical stance: running the business by moral principles, such as using only organic cotton.
  • Social entrepreneurship: trading to tackle a social or environmental problem.
  • Independence: being your own boss, with no manager above you.
  • Home working: running the business from home, which cuts costs and fits around childcare.

Non-financial motives come from the owner's values or the way they want to live.

cards.front: Explain why profit acts as an incentive to start a business.
cards.back:
An entrepreneur takes a risk that employees don't, and the chance of a profit is what makes the risk worth taking. Profit works as an incentive in three ways:

  • It rewards the owner: profit is the entrepreneur's income.
  • It pays for growth: profit kept in the business can fund new equipment, extra staff or a second site without borrowing.
  • It sends a signal: high profits → other entrepreneurs see money to be made → new firms enter → resources move to where consumers want them.

cards.front: Define the factors of production.
cards.back:
Factors of production — the resources used to make goods and provide services. Economists group them into four: land, labour, capital and enterprise.

Every business uses all four, but in a different mix: a farm needs a lot of land, a software firm hardly any. All four are scarce, so each has a price the business must pay to use it.

cards.front: Define enterprise as a factor of production.
cards.back:
Enterprise — the willingness and ability to organise the other factors of production and to take the risk of running a business.

The reward is profit, which, unlike the other rewards, is not agreed in advance and may be nothing at all.

cards.front: Define land as a factor of production. What does it include for a business?
cards.back:
Land — natural resources used in production, such as water, crops, timber and oil. For a business, land also includes its premises.

Raw materials count as land too, because they start as natural resources: the coffee beans a café buys began as a crop. The reward to land is rent.

cards.front: Define labour as a factor of production.
cards.back:
Labour — the physical and mental effort people put into production.

In a business, labour is its managers and employees. The reward is wages and salaries, paid whether the business does well or badly.

cards.front: Define capital as a factor of production.
cards.back:
Capital — man-made resources used in production, such as machinery, tools and vehicles.

In a business, capital is its equipment, such as a café's coffee machine, ovens, fridges and tills. The reward to capital is interest.

cards.front: A bakery uses: the shop it trades from, flour and eggs, ovens and mixers, its bakers, its shop manager, and the owner who opened it. Place each against its factor of production, and give each factor's reward.
cards.back:
Land (rent): the shop, which is its premises, and the flour and eggs, which are raw materials.

Capital (interest): the ovens and mixers, which are equipment.

Labour (wages and salaries): the bakers and the manager.

Enterprise (profit): the owner, who set up the business and takes the risk.

Owners are enterprise; managers and workers are labour.

cards.front: Define specialisation.
cards.back:
Specialisation — when a person, business, region or country concentrates on producing a narrow range of goods or services, or on one part of a production process.

A firm specialises when it concentrates on one product, one type of customer or one stage of production, such as a bakery that supplies only bread to supermarkets.

cards.front: Define the division of labour.
cards.back:
Division of labour — splitting production into separate tasks and giving each worker one task, or a small set of tasks, to do over and over.

It is specialisation inside a workplace. Adam Smith's pin factory (1776) is the classic example: ten workers sharing out the steps made upwards of 48,000 pins a day.

cards.front: Give the advantages and disadvantages of the division of labour to employers.
cards.back:
Advantages

  • Higher productivity: workers get faster with practice and waste no time switching between jobs.
  • Lower cost per unit: more output from the same wage bill.
  • Cheaper training: a new starter only has to learn one task.
  • Easier to use machinery: simple, repeated tasks suit specialist equipment.

Disadvantages

  • Boredom: repetitive work can lead to careless mistakes, lower quality and more days off sick.
  • Staff turnover: bored workers leave, and replacing them costs money.
  • Bottlenecks: if one worker is absent or slow, every later stage waits.
  • Less flexibility: staff who know one task cannot easily cover for others.

cards.front: Give the advantages and disadvantages of the division of labour to employees.
cards.back:
Advantages

  • Expertise: workers become highly skilled at their task.
  • Higher pay: skills that are in short supply can earn a premium.
  • Quicker start: less to learn before becoming useful in a new job.

Disadvantages

  • Monotony: the same task all day gives little job satisfaction.
  • Narrow skills: if the task is automated or the industry shrinks, the worker may struggle to find another job (structural unemployment).
  • Health: repeating the same movement can cause strain injuries.

Say whose advantage it is: higher productivity helps the employer, while the worker on the same line may find the job dull.

cards.front: Evaluate specialisation for a firm. What does whether it pays depend on?
cards.back:
Advantages: lower average costs from bulk buying and specialist machinery; a reputation for doing one thing well; cheaper marketing, with one clear message to one type of customer.

Disadvantages: all its eggs in one basket, so a fall in demand for its one product collapses sales; it depends on other firms for everything it doesn't make; specialist machinery and skills make it slow to adapt.

It depends on:

  • how stable demand is: safe in a steady market, risky where tastes or technology change fast;
  • the size of the market: the cost savings only come if it can sell a large volume;
  • trade: it needs reliable customers and suppliers.

cards.front: Define the interest rate.
cards.back:
Interest rate — the cost of borrowing money, or the reward for saving it, shown as a percentage of the amount borrowed or saved per year.

The Bank of England sets Bank Rate, which other interest rates follow.

cards.front: Define the exchange rate.
cards.back:
Exchange rate — the price of one currency in terms of another, such as £1 = $1.30.

Exchange rates are decided by currency markets. Remember SPICED: a Strong Pound makes Imports Cheap and Exports Dear.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how does a rise in interest rates affect a firm's costs, demand and investment?
cards.back:
Costs: rates rise → interest on variable-rate loans and overdrafts goes up → higher costs → lower profit for any firm that borrows.

Demand: rates rise → mortgage and credit-card repayments go up, and saving pays more → households spend less → lower sales, worst for things often bought on credit, such as cars and furniture.

Investment: rates rise → borrowing for a new machine or shop costs more → fewer projects earn enough to cover the interest → investment is delayed.

A cut in rates runs each chain the other way.

cards.front: A UK firm sells a £40 product to the US. The pound strengthens from £1 = $1.20 to £1 = $1.35. Calculate the dollar price before and after, and explain who gains and who loses.
cards.back:
Before: £40 × 1.20 = $48. After: £40 × 1.35 = $54.

SPICED: a Strong Pound makes Imports Cheap and Exports Dear.

  • Exporters lose: UK goods cost more abroad → overseas buyers switch to cheaper rivals → export sales and profit fall.
  • Importers gain: imported materials and components cost less in pounds → lower unit costs → higher margins.
  • Firms competing with imports lose: foreign goods get cheaper in UK shops.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how does a rise in inflation affect a firm?
cards.back:
• Costs: materials, energy and wages cost more → higher unit costs → lower margins unless the firm raises its prices.
  • Demand: prices rise faster than wages → real incomes fall → households buy less → lower sales.
  • Interest rates: the Bank of England raises rates to bring inflation down → the interest-rate chains follow.
  • Exports: UK prices rise faster than rivals' abroad → UK goods look expensive overseas → exporters lose sales.

How much it hurts depends on pricing power, since strong brands can usually pass costs on, and on whether wages keep up.

cards.front: Interest rates rise. Compare the effect on a heavily borrowed car dealer and a debt-free firm selling basic groceries.
cards.back:
The car dealer is hit from both sides. Its loan repayments rise, so its costs go up, unless it is on a fixed rate until the deal ends. And cars are often bought on credit, so its customers face dearer finance and its sales fall.

The grocer is barely touched. It has no loan to worry about, and households keep buying necessities. If it has cash in the bank, it earns more on it.

The effect always depends on the business: check its debts and whether it sells necessities or luxuries.

cards.front: Define demand.
cards.back:
Demand — the quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to buy at each price over a given period of time.

Both parts matter: wanting a new car is not demand unless you can pay for it. Demand backed by the ability to pay is effective demand.

cards.front: State the law of demand.
cards.back:
Law of demand — as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, ceteris paribus (all other things staying the same).

So the demand curve slopes down from left to right. When the price falls, buyers who could not afford the good before now can, existing buyers tend to buy more, and it looks cheaper next to its alternatives.

cards.front: Define real income, and explain the difference between a normal good and an inferior good.
cards.back:
Real income — income adjusted for inflation, so it measures what a consumer can actually buy.

  • Normal goods: demand rises as real income rises. Most goods are normal, such as holidays abroad.
  • Inferior goods: demand falls as real income rises, because people switch to something better. Supermarket value ranges are an example.

cards.front: Sketch an increase in demand, marking the quantity demanded at the original price. What could cause it?
cards.back:
The whole curve shifts right from D1 to D2, so more is bought at every price. At the same price P1, quantity demanded rises from Q1 to Q2.

Anything except the good's own price can cause it:

  • The price of a substitute rises.
  • The price of a complement falls.
  • Real incomes rise, for a normal good.
  • Tastes and fashions move towards it.
  • Advertising and branding work.
  • The population grows, or the age group that buys it gets larger.
cards.svgAlt: Two parallel downward-sloping demand curves, D1 and D2 to its right, with an arrow showing the shift right; at price P1 quantity demanded is Q1 on D1 and the larger Q2 on D2

cards.front:
Movement or shift? Say what happens to the demand curve for Brand X coffee pods when:

  1. the price of Brand X pods rises
  2. the pod coffee machines they fit are discounted
  3. a rival brand of pods cuts its price
  4. coffee becomes more fashionable.
cards.back:
1. Contraction along the curve. A good's own price never shifts its own demand curve.
  2. Shift right (an increase in demand). The machines are a complement, and a cheaper complement raises demand.
  3. Shift left (a decrease in demand). Rival pods are a substitute, and a cheaper substitute pulls buyers away.
  4. Shift right. Tastes have moved towards the product.

Keep the words apart: extension and contraction for movements, increase and decrease in demand for shifts.

cards.front: Define supply.
cards.back:
Supply — the quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at each price over a given period of time.

How much a producer makes depends on the price the product will sell for and what it costs to make. A higher price means more profit on each unit; higher costs mean less.

cards.front: State the law of supply, and explain why the supply curve slopes upwards.
cards.back:
Law of supply — as the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.

  • A higher price makes each unit more profitable, so existing producers want to sell more.
  • Extra output often costs more to make (overtime pay, older machines brought back into use), and only a higher price covers it.
  • Firms making other products are tempted to switch their resources into this one.

cards.front: Sketch an increase in supply, marking the quantity supplied at the original price. What could cause it?
cards.back:
The curve shifts right from S1 to S2, so more is offered for sale at every price. At the same price P, quantity supplied rises from Q1 to Q2.

Causes:

  • Lower costs of production: wages, raw materials, energy or rent.
  • New technology that makes more from the same inputs.
  • An indirect tax is cut or removed.
  • A subsidy is introduced or increased.
  • New firms enter the market.
  • A helpful external shock, such as a bumper harvest.

Each works in reverse to shift supply left.
cards.svgAlt: Two parallel upward-sloping supply curves, S1 and S2 to its right, with an arrow showing the shift right; at price P quantity supplied is Q1 on S1 and the larger Q2 on S2

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: the government puts a new indirect tax on a product. Which curve shifts, and why?
cards.back:
An indirect tax is a tax on spending, such as VAT or fuel duty, which the seller pays to the government.

The seller pays it → it adds to the cost of every unit → less profit on each unit → producers offer less at every price → supply shifts left.

The demand curve stays where it is, even though buyers end up paying a higher price.

A subsidy, a payment from the government to producers, works the other way: it lowers their costs, so supply shifts right.

cards.front: Define the equilibrium price.
cards.back:
Equilibrium price — the price at which the quantity consumers want to buy equals the quantity producers want to sell. It is also called the market-clearing price, because nothing is left unsold and no buyer who will pay that price goes without.

The equilibrium quantity is the amount bought and sold at that price. Once a market reaches equilibrium, there is no pressure for the price to change.

cards.front: Show excess demand on a supply and demand diagram, and explain how market forces remove it.
cards.back:
Excess demand: the quantity demanded is greater than the quantity supplied, because the price is below equilibrium. It shows up as a shortage.

At P1, below Pe, the excess is the horizontal gap between Qs and Qd.

Shops sell out and queues form → buyers will pay more and sellers see they can charge more → the price rises → demand contracts and supply extends (the arrows) → until the two are equal again at Pe.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with price P1 below the equilibrium price Pe; at P1 quantity supplied Qs is less than quantity demanded Qd, the gap is labelled excess demand, and arrows along both curves point up towards equilibrium

cards.front: Show excess supply on a supply and demand diagram, and explain how market forces remove it.
cards.back:
Excess supply: the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded, because the price is above equilibrium. It shows up as a surplus.

At P1, above Pe, the excess is the horizontal gap between Qd and Qs.

Sellers are left with unsold stock → they cut prices to clear it → demand extends and supply contracts (the arrows) → until the market clears at Pe.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with price P1 above the equilibrium price Pe; at P1 quantity demanded Qd is less than quantity supplied Qs, the gap is labelled excess supply, and arrows along both curves point down towards equilibrium

cards.front:
For each change, say which curve shifts and which way, and what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity:

  1. a celebrity is seen wearing a brand of trainers
  2. cheap flights abroad pull holidaymakers away from UK seaside resorts
  3. new robots cut the cost of making cars across the industry
  4. a drought cuts the coffee harvest.
cards.back:
1. Demand shifts right (tastes). Excess demand at the old price → P up, Q up.
  2. Demand for UK seaside holidays shifts left (a substitute got cheaper). Excess supply → P down, Q down.
  3. Supply shifts right (new technology). Excess supply → P down, Q up.
  4. Supply shifts left (an external shock). Excess demand → P up, Q down.

Use the same steps every time: name the factor, say which curve shifts and which way, explain the shortage or surplus at the old price, then state the new price and quantity.

cards.front: Give the limitations of the supply and demand model: why might a real market not behave as it predicts?
cards.back:
• Ceteris paribus rarely holds. Several things change at once. If demand and supply both rise, quantity goes up, but the price could go either way.
  • Time lags. Supply often cannot respond quickly: new houses take years to plan and build, so shortages can last.
  • Imperfect information. Nobody knows where the equilibrium is, so it is found by trial and error. People also buy out of habit or on impulse.
  • Non-price factors. Many firms compete on quality, brand and service, and change prices only now and then.
  • Markets that do not clear. Some prices are held away from equilibrium on purpose: big concert tickets are often priced below what fans would pay, so excess demand remains.

To evaluate, pick the limit that fits the case: a time lag for housing or crops, two curves shifting at once when several things change together.

cards.front: Define the price mechanism.
cards.back:
Price mechanism — the way changes in price, set by demand and supply, decide how a market's scarce resources are used.

Nobody is in charge. Prices rise and fall, buyers and sellers respond, and resources move to where they are wanted. This is the "invisible hand".

cards.front: Name and explain the three functions of the price mechanism.
cards.back:
• Rationing: when something is scarce, a higher price limits it to those willing and able to pay the most.
  • Incentive: a higher price means more profit, which encourages firms to produce more.
  • Signalling: a price change tells buyers and sellers that conditions have changed. A rising price shows demand is outrunning supply.

Keep signalling and incentive apart. The signal is the information: the price has risen, so demand is up. The incentive is the reason to act on it: higher prices mean more profit.

cards.front: Demand for a firm's product rises. Build the chains of reasoning for its three possible responses, and say what decides which one it chooses.
cards.back:
• Raise its price: stock runs short → the firm raises its price → the higher price rations what it has → more profit on each sale.
  • Produce more with what it has: spare capacity, overtime or stock → supply extends → higher revenue.
  • Invest in more capacity: the rise looks set to last → new staff, machinery or premises → higher output and new jobs.

It depends on whether the rise will last (no firm builds capacity for a heatwave), how much spare capacity the firm has, and what rivals do: if they hold their prices, raising its own risks losing customers.

In the longer run, higher profits attract new firms → supply shifts right → the price is pushed back down.

cards.front: Define a niche market, and compare it with a mass market.
cards.back:
Niche market — a small, specialised part of a larger market, with customers who want something particular, such as gluten-free bread or kit for left-handed golfers.

A mass market is a large market where similar products are sold to most types of customer, such as toothpaste, crisps or smartphones.

  • Mass: many buyers and usually several large sellers → competition keeps prices close to each other → small profit on each unit, so firms rely on high volumes at low cost.
  • Niche: fewer competitors, and customers will often pay more for a product that suits them → profit on each unit can be high, but sales are small. If the niche grows, its profits draw in bigger firms and prices fall.

cards.front: A market's sales rise from £25m to £28m in a year. Calculate the market growth, and give two signs that a market has room to grow.
cards.back:
Market growth (%) = change in market size ÷ original market size × 100 = £3m ÷ £25m × 100 = 12%.

A growing market lets a firm raise sales without taking customers from rivals. Signs of room to grow:

  • prices and profits rising, a signal that demand is outrunning supply
  • changing tastes, or growth in the age group that buys the product
  • rising real incomes, for normal goods
  • new technology that creates a product or makes it cheaper.

cards.front: Define primary research, and give one advantage and one drawback.
cards.back:
Primary research — new information collected first-hand by the business, for its own purpose. It is also called field research.

Methods include surveys, interviews, focus groups and test marketing, where a product is sold in one area before a full launch.

For: up to date, fits the firm's exact question, and not available to rivals. Against: often slow and expensive to collect.

cards.front: Define secondary research, and give one advantage and one drawback.
cards.back:
Secondary research — using information that has already been collected by someone else, or for another purpose. It is also called desk research.

Sources include the Office for National Statistics (ONS), published market reports, competitors' websites and the firm's own sales records.

For: quick and cheap. Against: may be out of date, may not answer the firm's exact question, and rivals can read it too.

cards.front: Define quantitative data and qualitative data.
cards.back:
Quantitative data — information that can be counted or measured, such as how many people would buy a product or how much they would pay. It is used to estimate demand and sales.

Qualitative data — information about opinions, feelings and reasons, such as why customers prefer one brand to another. It explains behaviour but is hard to turn into numbers.

Do not mix up the two pairs. Primary or secondary is about who collected the data; quantitative or qualitative is about what kind of data it is. One survey can be primary and give both.

cards.front: Define market segmentation, and give the usual ways to segment a market.
cards.back:
Market segmentation — dividing a market into groups of customers who share similar characteristics and needs, so a firm can target one or more of them.

  • Demographic: age, gender or family size.
  • Geographic: where people live.
  • Income: how much customers can spend.
  • Lifestyle: interests, values and habits.

It lets a firm design products, prices and adverts for the people most likely to buy, so less marketing money is wasted. The risk is that targeting one segment closely can put off customers outside it.

cards.front: Explain the limitations of market research, including sample size and bias.
cards.back:
Sample size. A firm cannot ask everyone, so it asks a sample. The smaller the sample, the more likely the results are down to chance. A bigger one is more reliable but costs more and takes longer.

Bias makes results lean one way, so they no longer give a true picture of the market. It creeps in through:

  • who is asked, such as only the firm's social media followers
  • how the question is worded, such as a question that pushes people towards yes
  • what people say: saying you would buy is not the same as buying
  • who reads the results: an owner keen on the idea may pay most attention to the answers that support it.

Even good research goes out of date as tastes change, and it cannot predict what rivals will do next.

cards.front: Define market positioning.
cards.back:
Market positioning — where a product sits in customers' minds compared with its rivals, for example cheap and basic, or expensive and high quality.

Positions can be compared on a market map — a diagram that plots the brands in a market against two features customers care about, such as price and quality.

cards.front: Sketch a market map showing a gap in the market. How can a firm use one, and what are its limits?
cards.back:
Brands are plotted against two features customers care about, here price and quality. The circled space at below-average price and above-average quality is a gap in the market: a position no brand fills.

Uses: see which brands are the closest competitors, spot a gap, and decide where to place a new product or whether to move an existing one.

Limits: where each brand goes is often a judgement call, and two features cannot capture everything customers weigh up. A gap is not proof of demand: ask whether customers want it and whether the firm can serve it at a profit.

cards.front: Define competitive advantage, and give the two broad routes to it.
cards.back:
Competitive advantage — something that lets a business attract customers away from its rivals and earn higher profits than they do.

  • Lower costs: charge less than rivals and still make a profit, or charge the same and make more. Discount supermarkets such as Aldi and Lidl compete this way.
  • A better product, or one customers see as better, so they will pay more for it.

It is worth most when it is hard to copy. A strong brand, a patent, a prime location or highly skilled staff take rivals years to match; a price cut can be matched the next day.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does product differentiation raise a firm's profit margins?
cards.back:
Product differentiation is making a product different from rival products in ways that customers value: design, features, quality, packaging, branding or after-sales service. The aim is often a unique selling point (USP).

A differentiated product has fewer close substitutes → customers are less likely to switch when its price goes up → the firm can charge more without losing many sales → higher profit margins.

It is also how firms add value. The beans, milk and cup in a latte cost a small part of its price: customers are paying for the skill, the brand and the convenience.

cards.front: Define a stable market and a dynamic market, and explain how competing differs in each.
cards.back:
Stable market — a market where sales, products and customer tastes change little from year to year, such as bread, toilet roll or milk.

Dynamic market — a market that changes quickly, with new products, new technology and shifting tastes, such as smartphones, fashion or video games.

  • Stable: planning is easier, but growth is hard. A firm mostly gains sales by taking them from rivals, so it competes on cost, price and brand loyalty.
  • Dynamic: more chances to grow, but more risk. Firms must keep researching customers and developing products, because today's best seller can be overtaken within a year or two.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define a financial intermediary, and explain why savers and firms need one.
cards.back:
Financial intermediary — an organisation, such as a bank, that takes in money from savers and lends it to borrowers.

Savers deposit money and are paid interest on it. The bank lends that money on to firms that want to invest, and charges them interest. Without banks, this would be much harder:

  • savers want to be able to take their money out at short notice, while firms want to borrow for years
  • one saver lending to one firm could lose everything if that firm failed, whereas a bank spreads its lending across thousands of borrowers
  • most savers have no way of judging whether a business is likely to repay.

Across the economy, savings end up paying for investment, which raises firms' capacity and productivity.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define credit. Why do firms borrow, and how does a bank decide whether to lend?
cards.back:
Credit — money lent to a household or firm that has to be paid back later, usually with interest.

Firms borrow to start up before they have any sales, to cover a gap between paying bills and being paid, or to invest in more capacity than their profits can pay for.

Before lending, a bank checks how likely the borrower is to repay, usually from a business plan, a cash-flow forecast and the firm's credit history.

Banks make most of their profit from the gap between the interest they charge borrowers and the interest they pay savers. So a bank wants to lend, but only to borrowers it expects to pay it back.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define the interest rate, and explain how the general level of interest rates affects saving and investment.
cards.back:
Interest rate — the cost of borrowing money, or the reward for saving it, shown as a percentage of the amount borrowed or saved per year.

Low rates → saving earns little and borrowing is cheap → households save less and firms invest more.

High rates do the opposite: saving earns more and borrowing costs more, so households save more and firms invest less.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: A firm borrows £50,000 at an interest rate of 6% a year. Calculate the interest it pays in the first year. How much more would it pay at 9%?
cards.back:
Interest = £50,000 × 6% = £3,000 in the first year, on top of repaying the £50,000 itself.

At 9%: £50,000 × 9% = £4,500, which is £1,500 more.

The higher the rate, the more each project has to earn to be worth borrowing for.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front:
For each pair, say which a bank would charge the higher interest rate, and why:

  1. a new café with no track record, or a café chain that has traded for 20 years
  2. a loan secured on the firm's warehouse, or the same loan with no security
  3. an overdraft, or a loan
  4. a new loan taken out before, or after, the Bank of England raises Bank Rate.
cards.back:
1. The new café (risk of the borrower). With no track record it is more likely to default, so the bank charges a higher rate to cover that chance.
  2. The unsecured loan (collateral). A secured loan is cheaper, because the bank can recover its money if the borrower fails to pay.
  3. The overdraft (type of loan). Overdrafts usually cost more than loans.
  4. After the rise (Bank Rate). Banks pay more to borrow themselves, so they charge more on new loans and overdrafts.

The other factor is the length of the loan: money lent for longer is exposed to more things going wrong.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define collateral. Why does it make borrowing harder for new and small firms?
cards.back:
Collateral — an asset a borrower promises to a lender, which the lender can take and sell if the loan is not repaid.

Property is the most common collateral, but machinery, vehicles and stock can also be used. A loan backed by collateral is a secured loan; one without is an unsecured loan. Collateral lowers the bank's risk, so it makes lending more likely and cheaper.

New and small firms have few assets → little to offer as security → the bank asks the owner for a personal guarantee, a promise to repay from their own money, sometimes backed by their home → if the business fails, the owner can lose personal assets as well as the business.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define risk in business. Why do entrepreneurs accept it?
cards.back:
Risk — the chance that a decision turns out worse than expected, so that a business makes a loss or fails.

Every business takes risks, and starting one is the biggest risk of all: the owner puts in time and money before knowing whether anyone will buy.

Entrepreneurs accept risk because of the possible reward. Profit is the return for taking it. In general, the riskier the venture, the higher the profit needed to make it worth trying.

Lenders and investors face risk too: a bank may not get its money back, which is why riskier borrowers are charged higher interest.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define unlimited liability and limited liability. How does a business get limited liability?
cards.back:
Unlimited liability — the owners are personally responsible for all of the business's debts, with no limit.

Limited liability — the owners can lose no more than the money they have put into the business.

With unlimited liability, the law treats the owner and the business as the same thing. If the business cannot pay its debts, the people it owes can take the owner's savings, car or house.

A business gets limited liability by becoming a company, a separate legal entity: it owns its own assets, signs its own contracts and owes its own debts. The owners are shareholders. If the company fails, they lose the value of their shares, but its debts are not theirs to pay.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Name the four types of business ownership, and give the liability and access to finance of each.
cards.back:
• Sole trader: unlimited liability. One person owns and usually runs the business. Finance comes from the owner's savings, bank loans and overdrafts, so large sums are hard to raise.
  • Partnership: unlimited liability. Two or more partners share ownership, decisions and profit. Each partner can put money in, so more than a sole trader, but still limited.
  • Private limited company (Ltd): limited liability. Shareholders are often family and friends, and shares cannot be offered to the public. It can sell shares to chosen investors, and banks lend more readily to an established company.
  • Public limited company (plc): limited liability. Shareholders can be anyone if the shares are listed on a stock exchange. It can sell shares to the public, and needs at least £50,000 of share capital.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how does limited liability help owners, help firms raise finance, and help the economy?
cards.back:
• Owners: losses capped at what they put in → they can start and grow a business without betting their home on it → more people are willing to take the risk.
  • Raising finance: the most an investor can lose is what they paid for their shares → people will buy shares in a company they do not run → a company can raise far more outside finance.
  • The economy: the downside is capped → more businesses are started and more money is invested in them → more jobs and growth.

This is why a business that wants large amounts of outside finance becomes a company.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Does becoming a limited company make a business safer? Evaluate, including what it means for lenders and suppliers.
cards.back:
Limited liability protects the owners, not the business. A limited company can still run out of cash and close. What changes is how much the owners lose when it does: what they put in, and no more.

Risk moves to the people the company owes → if it fails, they may get back only part of what they are owed → banks often ask the directors of a small company for a personal guarantee, and suppliers may give a new company less time to pay.

Unlimited liability is simpler: a sole trader can start straight away, with no forms to file, and keeps their accounts private. But a failed business can leave the owner with debts for years.

A limited company must file its accounts at Companies House, where anyone can read them. That helps lenders and suppliers judge how safe it is to deal with.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define a loan and an overdraft, and say what each one suits.
cards.back:
Loan — a fixed sum borrowed for an agreed period and repaid in regular instalments, with interest.

Overdraft — an arrangement that lets a business take its bank account below zero, up to an agreed limit.

  • Loan: suits a one-off purchase that will earn money over several years, such as a delivery van. The repayments are known in advance, but they must be made every month whatever sales are like, and the bank may want collateral.
  • Overdraft: flexible. The firm pays interest only on what it is overdrawn by, and only while it is overdrawn, so it suits short gaps between paying bills and being paid. But the rate is usually higher than on a loan, and the bank can cut the limit at short notice.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define trade credit. What are its benefits and its risks?
cards.back:
Trade credit — when a supplier lets a business take goods now and pay for them later, often 30 or 60 days later.

For: it costs nothing if the bill is paid on time, and a shop can sometimes sell the goods before it has to pay for them.

Against: a business that pays late may be charged extra, refused credit next time or lose the supplier altogether.

Banks are not the only source of credit. Suppliers give trade credit, and specialist finance companies lend for vehicles and equipment, often using the item itself as security.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define venture capital. Which firms use it, and what does it cost them?
cards.back:
Venture capital — money that specialist investment firms put into a small, fast-growing business, taking part ownership of it in exchange.

Venture capitalists back firms that are too risky for a bank but could grow very large, often in technology. They usually bring advice and contacts as well as money.

The cost: they take a large stake, and often a say in how the business is run.

It is not borrowed, so it is an alternative to credit. Business angels are similar: wealthy people who invest their own money in small firms for a share of the business.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define share capital. What is its main advantage, and what does it cost the owners?
cards.back:
Share capital — money raised by selling shares in a company to investors, who become part owners.

For: it never has to be repaid and carries no interest.

The cost is control: each new shareholder owns part of the business and expects a share of the profit as dividends.

Only companies can raise it, and only a plc can sell shares to the public.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define leasing, and give one advantage and one drawback.
cards.back:
Leasing — paying to use an asset, such as a vehicle or a photocopier, for a set period without buying it.

For: it avoids a large payment up front, and the lease may include repairs.

Against: over the life of the asset it usually costs more than buying, and the business never owns it.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Define owner's capital, and explain the three sources of internal finance.
cards.back:
Owner's capital — money the owners put into the business themselves.

Finance is internal if it comes from inside the business and external if it comes from outside.

  • Personal savings: the most common way to start a small business. There is no interest to pay and no one else to answer to, but most people do not have much, and the owner can lose it all.
  • Retained profit: profit kept in the business rather than paid out to the owners. It is the cheapest finance for an established firm, but a new business has none, and every pound kept is a pound the owners do not receive.
  • Sale of assets: raising money from things the business no longer needs, such as an empty warehouse or old equipment. It can only be done once per asset.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front:
Recommend a source of finance for each business, and justify it:

  1. a caterer that must pay its staff this month but will not be paid for a wedding until next month
  2. a profitable printing firm that has traded for 30 years, replacing one of its machines
  3. a new two-person software start-up with no trading record or profits, which could grow very large
  4. a manufacturing company building a new factory.
cards.back:
1. Overdraft. A short-term gap needs short-term finance, and an overdraft charges interest only while the firm is overdrawn.
  2. Retained profit. It is the cheapest finance for an established firm, and this one has profits to use.
  3. Venture capital or business angels. With no trading record, it is too risky for a bank, but its growth potential attracts investors. The price is a share of the business.
  4. A bank loan or share capital. A long-term asset suits long-term finance.

Match the finance to what it is for. A recommendation that is not linked to the firm's situation picks up few evaluation marks.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: why do small and new businesses find it hardest to get credit, and where else can they turn?
cards.back:
A bank wants to know the borrower can repay, and a start-up cannot prove it:

  • it has no trading record, credit history or past accounts
  • it often has few assets to offer as collateral
  • the owner knows far more about the business than the bank does, so the bank cannot easily tell a good plan from a weak one.

→ the firm may be refused, offered less than it asked for, or charged a high interest rate. Credit is also harder to get when banks are cautious, as in a recession, just when many firms need it most.

Other routes: business angels; crowdfunding, where many people each put in a small amount over the internet for a reward or a small share of the business; and peer-to-peer lending, where individuals lend to a business through a website and are paid interest, with no bank in between.

cards.topic: 1.4 The Role of Credit in the Economy
cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning for the impact of credit on the economy: when it flows easily, when there is too much, and when it dries up. What decides how much a change in credit matters?
cards.back:
• Credit flows easily: firms borrow to invest in equipment and premises, and households to buy houses and cars → more spending → more demand for other businesses → they hire more workers → investment and growth.
  • Too much credit: households and firms borrow more than they can repay → a rise in interest rates or a fall in income leaves them unable to keep up the payments → spending falls sharply, and the banks that lent to them make losses.
  • Credit dries up: the first chain runs in reverse. A bakery is refused a loan for a second oven: the oven maker loses a sale, and the bakery does not hire the extra baker it needed. When banks turn down thousands of firms at once, spending and jobs fall across the economy.

It depends on how much firms rely on borrowing (a firm that can invest out of retained profit barely notices when banks become cautious; a start-up with no profit has no such cushion) and on confidence (easy credit only raises investment if firms expect demand to hold up).

cards.front: Define private costs, external costs and social costs, and give the link between them.
cards.back:
Private costs — the costs paid by the firm or person carrying out an activity, such as a firm's wages, materials and energy, or the price a consumer pays for a good.

External costs — costs that fall on a third party, someone outside the transaction, who is not compensated for them. Noise, pollution and congestion are the usual examples.

Social costs — the full cost of an activity to society, which is the private cost plus any external cost.

Social cost = private cost + external cost

cards.front: Define private benefits, external benefits and social benefits, and give the link between them.
cards.back:
Private benefits — the benefits that go to the person or firm who buys, uses or makes something, such as the enjoyment a consumer gets from a good or the revenue a firm earns from selling it.

External benefits — gains that go to third parties, who do not pay for them.

Social benefits — the full benefit of an activity to society, which is the private benefit plus any external benefit.

Social benefit = private benefit + external benefit

cards.front: Define an externality. Name the four types, by whether a firm or a consumer causes them, with an example of each.
cards.back:
Externality — an external cost or external benefit. A negative externality is an external cost and a positive externality is an external benefit.

  • External cost of production (a firm, while making a good): water companies releasing sewage into rivers and the sea.
  • External cost of consumption (a consumer, while using a good): drivers adding to congestion and air pollution for everyone else on the road.
  • External benefit of production (a firm, while making a good): a firm trains its staff, some of whom later take those skills to other employers.
  • External benefit of consumption (a consumer, while using a good): a vaccinated person is less likely to pass a disease on.

The people causing an externality do not have to think about it, so decisions are made on private costs and benefits alone.

cards.front: Define market failure and the social optimum. When does a free market reach the social optimum on its own?
cards.back:
Market failure — when the free market leads to too much or too little of a good being produced or consumed, so resources are not allocated in the best way for society.

Social optimum — the output where the social cost of one more unit equals its social benefit, written MSC = MSB on a diagram. The last unit made costs society exactly what it is worth to society.

In most markets there is no externality, so private and social costs and benefits are the same. The market equilibrium is then the social optimum, and the market works well on its own.

When there is an externality, the two points split apart: the market ends up at Q1 when society would be better off at Q2.

cards.front: A paper mill spends £70 to make each tonne of paper. Chemicals it releases into a river cause £20 of damage per tonne to fishing firms downstream, who are not compensated. Calculate the social cost per tonne, and explain why the market produces too much paper.
cards.back:
Social cost = private cost + external cost = £70 + £20 = £90 a tonne.

The mill prices from its own £70 → paper sells for less than its cost to society → more is bought → the fishing firms bear the £20.

This is an external cost of production, so the market produces more than the social optimum: overproduction.

cards.front: Sketch the diagram for an external cost of production. Mark the market outcome, the social optimum and the welfare loss.
cards.back:
MSC lies above S=MPC, and the gap between them is the external cost of each unit. Demand is D=MPB=MSB.

  • Market: where supply meets demand, at P1 and Q1.
  • Social optimum: where MSC meets demand, at P2 and Q2. Q1 is more than Q2, so there is overproduction.
  • Welfare loss: between Q2 and Q1, each extra unit costs society more than it is worth to buyers, and P1 is too low because it leaves out the external cost. The shaded triangle is the welfare loss.

Example: a factory's fumes harming the health of people nearby.
cards.svgAlt: Externality diagram with MSC above S=MPC and demand labelled D=MPB=MSB; the market is at P1 and Q1, the social optimum at P2 and the smaller Q2, and a shaded welfare loss triangle lies between Q2 and Q1

cards.front: Sketch the diagram for an external benefit of consumption, such as a vaccine. Mark the market outcome, the social optimum and the welfare loss.
cards.back:
MSB lies above D=MPB, because using the good helps other people. Supply is S=MPC=MSC.

  • Market: consumers buy Q1, where D=MPB meets supply, at P1. Someone deciding whether to have a vaccine thinks about their own health, not the people they would no longer infect.
  • Social optimum: where MSB meets supply, at P2 and Q2. Q1 is less than Q2, so there is underconsumption.
  • Welfare loss: the shaded triangle is the benefit society misses out on: units between Q1 and Q2 that would have been worth more to society than they cost to make.

The externality does not shift supply or demand. MSB is an extra line that shows what the market leaves out, so the market stays at Q1.
cards.svgAlt: Externality diagram with MSB above D=MPB and supply labelled S=MPC=MSC; the market is at P1 and Q1, the social optimum at P2 and the larger Q2, and a shaded welfare loss triangle lies between Q1 and Q2

cards.front:
For each, name the type of externality, say where the social curve sits, and say whether the free market gives too much or too little:

  1. a cement works whose dust settles on nearby homes and cars
  2. smokers whose smoke harms the people around them
  3. a building firm that trains apprentices, many of whom later work for other builders
  4. adults who take a first-aid course and can then help strangers in an emergency.
cards.back:
1. External cost of production. MSC above S=MPC → overproduction.
  2. External cost of consumption. MSB below D=MPB → overconsumption.
  3. External benefit of production. MSC below S=MPC → underproduction.
  4. External benefit of consumption. MSB above D=MPB → underconsumption.

External costs give too much; external benefits give too little. In every case the market stays at Q1, where S=MPC meets D=MPB.

cards.front: Define legislation and regulation as methods of government intervention. Give the main strength and drawback of each.
cards.back:
Legislation — laws passed by Parliament that ban or require something. Since 1 June 2025 it has been illegal for shops in England to sell single-use vapes, which were being thrown away as litter in large numbers.

Regulation — rules that control how firms operate, set and enforced by government bodies, usually under powers that legislation gives them. Emission limits on factories, food hygiene inspections and safety standards are all regulation. A firm that breaks the rules can be fined or shut down.

  • Legislation: clear and quick to understand, and can stop a harmful product outright. But it needs enforcing, and a ban can push sales to an illegal market.
  • Regulation: can be set for each industry and updated as technology changes. But inspecting and enforcing costs money, and firms face paperwork and compliance costs.

cards.front: Define an indirect tax. How can it correct overproduction? Give a UK example.
cards.back:
Indirect tax — a tax on spending, paid to the government by the seller and added to the cost of each unit. It raises the price and cuts the quantity bought.

If the tax equals the external cost of each unit, overproduction is corrected.

Example: the Soft Drinks Industry Levy, since April 2018. Producers pay it on soft drinks with 5g or more of sugar per 100ml, and many brands cut the sugar to pay less or none.

cards.front: Define a subsidy and a grant. How can a subsidy correct underconsumption, and what is its main drawback?
cards.back:
Subsidy — a payment from the government to producers that lowers their cost of each unit, so they supply more at a lower price. A grant is a one-off payment for a set purpose, such as the Boiler Upgrade Scheme's £7,500 towards a heat pump for homes in England and Wales.

If the subsidy matches the external benefit of each unit, output rises towards the social optimum and underconsumption is corrected.

Drawback: it costs the government money that could be spent elsewhere, such as on schools or hospitals, which is an opportunity cost. A firm that has been subsidised for years may also feel less pressure to cut its costs.

cards.front: Define a voluntary agreement. Give its main strength and its main drawback.
cards.back:
Voluntary agreement — a promise by firms in an industry to change what they do, agreed with the government with no law forcing them. In 2016 the food industry was asked to cut sugar in foods such as cereals, yoghurts and biscuits by 20% by 2020, on a voluntary basis.

  • Strength: cheap to run, and firms can choose the cheapest way to meet the target.
  • Drawback: nothing happens to firms that ignore the target. The sugar programme cut the sugar in the foods it covered by far less than its target.

cards.front: Define government failure, and outline its four causes.
cards.back:
Government failure — when government intervention makes the allocation of resources worse than it was before, or costs more than the benefit it brings.

  • Distortion of price signals: a tax or subsidy changes the price, so the signal it sends firms about what consumers want can point the wrong way.
  • Unintended consequences: people and firms respond to a policy in ways the government did not plan for.
  • Excessive administrative costs: designing, running and enforcing a policy costs money, and if those costs are high compared with what it achieves, society can end up worse off.
  • Information gaps: the government rarely knows the external cost for sure, so a tax can be set too high or too low.

cards.front: Sketch an indirect tax on a supply and demand diagram. Mark the tax per unit, how it is split between buyers and producers, and the government's revenue.
cards.back:
A tax of a set amount per unit adds to the seller's costs, so supply shifts up and to the left, from S to S+Tax. The price buyers pay rises from P1 to P2, and the quantity falls from Q1 to Q2. Producers keep P3.

  • Tax per unit: the full vertical gap from P3 to P2, measured at Q2 between the two supply curves.
  • Who pays: buyers pay P1 to P2 through the higher price, and producers pay P1 to P3 through the lower amount they keep.
  • Revenue: tax per unit × Q2, the shaded rectangle from P3 up to P2 and across to Q2.

A common slip is to mark P1 to P2 as the tax. That is only the part buyers pay.

cards.front: Sketch a subsidy on a supply and demand diagram. Mark the subsidy per unit and the cost to the government.
cards.back:
A subsidy lowers each unit's cost, so supply shifts down and to the right, from S to S+Subsidy. The price buyers pay falls from P1 to P2, and the quantity rises from Q1 to Q2. Producers receive P3 per unit, including the subsidy.

  • Subsidy per unit: the gap between P3 and P2.
  • Cost to the government: that gap × Q2, the shaded rectangle.

The government has to fund that rectangle from taxes or borrowing.

cards.front: Evaluate an indirect tax as a way to cut the consumption of a good with external costs.
cards.back:
For

  • It makes the polluter pay and raises revenue, while buyers and firms still choose for themselves.
  • It can change what firms make. While the voluntary sugar programme fell well short of its target, brands cut the sugar in soft drinks much further to pay less of the levy.

Against

  • Hard to set at the right level. If the damage from each unit is 20p but the tax is 50p, output is cut by too much. Set it too low and overproduction carries on.
  • Little effect if buyers keep buying. Smokers keep buying cigarettes when the price rises, so a tobacco tax raises a lot of revenue but cuts smoking less than it might.
  • Unintended consequences. Heavy duty on cigarettes has moved some of the market underground, which limits how high the tax can usefully go.
  • It takes a larger share of a poorer household's income.

Judgement: how far a tax works depends on how much buyers react to the higher price.

cards.front:
Name the cause of government failure in each case, and explain it:

  1. the government pays dairy farmers for every litre of milk they produce, and they produce more milk than people want to buy
  2. a very high tax on bottles of spirits leads to a trade in smuggled, untaxed spirits
  3. an insulation grant has such complicated forms that a large share of its budget goes on staff checking applications
  4. a tax on a pesticide is set at £5 a litre, but the damage each litre does turns out to be £2.
cards.back:
1. Distortion of price signals. Farmers respond to the subsidy as well as to demand, so the surplus has to be stored or wasted.
  2. Unintended consequences. The smuggled spirits are sold cheaply and pay no tax, so some of the harm the tax was meant to cut comes back in another form.
  3. Excessive administrative costs. The cost of running the scheme is high compared with what it achieves. The UK's Green Homes Grant (2020 to 2021) was a real case: it was too complicated.
  4. Information gaps. The tax is set above the external cost, so output is cut by too much and society loses goods that were worth making.

cards.front: Define sales volume and sales revenue, and give the link between them.
cards.back:
Sales volume — the number of units a business sells in a period, such as a week, a month or a year.

Sales revenue — the money a business receives from selling its output, before any costs are taken off. It is also called total revenue or turnover.

Sales revenue = Price × Sales volume, which rearranges to Sales volume = Sales revenue ÷ Price.

Revenue is not profit: costs still have to be paid.

cards.front: Define fixed costs and variable costs, with examples of each.
cards.back:
Fixed costs — costs that do not change when output changes, at least in the short run. Rent, business rates, insurance and the salaries of permanent staff are all fixed costs. They have to be paid even in a month when the business makes nothing.

Variable costs — costs that rise and fall with output. Raw materials, packaging, the energy used by machines and delivery charges are variable costs. Make nothing and they fall to zero.

Total variable costs = variable cost of one unit × output.

cards.front: Define total costs and average cost, and give the formula for each.
cards.back:
Total costs — the whole cost of producing a given level of output, found by adding fixed and variable costs:

Total costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs

Average cost — the cost of producing one unit, found by dividing total costs by output:

Average cost = Total costs ÷ Output

It is also called unit cost.

cards.front: State the formula for percentage change. A gym's members fall from 800 to 680: what is the percentage change?
cards.back:
Take the change, divide it by the original value and multiply by 100: (680 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100 = −15%. A negative answer means a fall.

Always divide by the original value. If members go back up from 680 to 800, the rise is 120 ÷ 680 × 100 = 17.6%, not 15%, because the starting figure is smaller.

Take care with figures that are already percentages: an interest rate going from 2% to 3% has risen by one percentage point, which is a 50% increase.

cards.front:
A bakery has fixed costs of £3,000 a month. Each loaf uses £1.50 of flour and packaging.

Calculate total costs and average cost at 1,000 and at 4,000 loaves a month. Why does average cost fall?
cards.back:
• 1,000 loaves: variable costs 1,000 × £1.50 = £1,500. Total costs £3,000 + £1,500 = £4,500. Average cost £4,500 ÷ 1,000 = £4.50.
  • 4,000 loaves: variable costs 4,000 × £1.50 = £6,000. Total costs £3,000 + £6,000 = £9,000. Average cost £9,000 ÷ 4,000 = £2.25.

Average cost falls because the same £3,000 of fixed costs is shared across more loaves: £3 a loaf at 1,000, but only 75p at 4,000.

Fixed costs are only fixed up to a point. If the bakery grows enough to need bigger premises, they jump to a new level.

cards.front: Define contribution per unit. What does contribution go towards?
cards.back:
Contribution per unit — the selling price of one unit minus its variable cost:

Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit

It is what is left from each sale once its variable cost is paid. It goes towards the fixed costs, and once they are covered, the contribution from every further unit is profit.

Total contribution = contribution per unit × sales volume. Take fixed costs away from it and you have profit.

cards.front: Define the break-even point.
cards.back:
Break-even point — the level of output at which total revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss. At that output, total fixed costs + total variable costs = total sales revenue.

Below the break-even point the business makes a loss. Above it, the business makes a profit.

cards.front: Define the margin of safety. What does it tell a business?
cards.back:
Margin of safety — the amount by which actual or planned sales are above the break-even point:

Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output

It shows how far sales could fall before the business makes a loss, in units or as a percentage of actual sales. A large margin means it could survive a drop in demand; a small one means even a short dip would push it into loss.

cards.front: Sketch a break-even chart. Label fixed costs, total costs, total revenue, the break-even point, the areas of loss and profit, and the margin of safety.
cards.back:
Output goes along the bottom, and costs and revenue go up the side.

  • FC is a horizontal line: it is the same at every output.
  • TC starts at the fixed cost line, because some costs are paid even at zero output, and rises with each unit made.
  • TR starts at zero and rises more steeply than TC, because each unit sells for more than its variable cost.
  • The break-even point is where TR crosses TC. The gap between them to the left is a loss, and to the right a profit.
  • The margin of safety runs from break-even output to actual output.

Here fixed costs are £2,000, the firm breaks even at 250 units and £3,000, and actual output of 500 gives a margin of safety of 250.

cards.front:
A food truck sells burritos for £9 each. Each burrito costs £3.50 in ingredients and packaging, and the truck's fixed costs are £4,400 a month. It sells 1,100 burritos a month.

Calculate contribution per unit, break-even output, break-even revenue, the margin of safety and monthly profit.
cards.back:
• Contribution per unit: £9 − £3.50 = £5.50
  • Break-even output: £4,400 ÷ £5.50 = 800 burritos
  • Break-even revenue: 800 × £9 = £7,200
  • Margin of safety: 1,100 − 800 = 300 burritos, which is 27.3% of sales
  • Profit: the contribution from the 300 burritos sold beyond break-even, 300 × £5.50 = £1,650

Check: revenue of 1,100 × £9 = £9,900, minus total costs of £4,400 + (1,100 × £3.50) = £8,250, also gives £1,650.

Divide fixed costs by contribution, not by the selling price. £4,400 ÷ £9 gives 489, which ignores the £3.50 each burrito costs to make.
